response.answer: If your spouse dies, you may be eligible for survivor benefits based on their work record. Generally, you can receive survivor benefits as a widow/widower if you are at least age 60 (age 50 if disabled), or at any age if you are caring for their child who is under 16 or disabled. [探索您可能有权获得的福利 > 联系社会保障局]
您或您的家人可能有资格获得增加的福利

我们的使命是提供满足公众不断变化需求的社会保障服务。

福利领取者的状况在申请或符合福利资格后发生变化并不罕见。如果您或您的家人领取社会保障或 补充保障收入（SSI），某些生活变化可能会影响您获得联邦福利增加的资格。例如，如果您的配 偶或前配偶去世，您可能有资格获得更高的社会保障福利。

要了解您或您的家人是否可能基于他人的工作记录而有资格获得福利，或基于您自己的工作记录获 得更高的福利，请参阅社会保障网站上的福利信息。您还可以使用福利资格筛选工具（BEST）来 了解您是否可以获得社会保障管理局管理的福利。根据您对问题的回答，该工具将列出您可能有资 格获得的福利，并告诉您有关如何符合资格和申请的更多信息。

以下问题和答案涉及一些可能增加您福利的生活变化。

您的配偶或前配偶是否已去世？

如果您的配偶或前配偶已去世，您可能有资格基于他或她的工作记录获得更高的遗属福利。即使您 已经在领取基于另一位配偶的遗属福利，前配偶的去世也可能使您有资格获得更高的遗属福利。

您是否正在领取基于您自己工作记录的医疗保险福利，其中包括至少10年您缴纳社会保障税的收入 ？

如果您年满65岁，您可能有资格基于自己的记录领取现金福利。如果您已达到完全退休年龄或以上 ，无论您赚多少钱，您都可以工作并领取每月的社会保障福利。请查阅本出版物以了解更多信息。

您那个曾帮助抚养您的成年子女是否已去世？

如果您的子女有足够的工作积分，并且曾提供您至少一半的生活费，您可能有资格基于他或她的工 作记录获得更高的父母福利。

您是否正在领取基于您配偶工作记录的社会保障福利？

如果您工作过，您可能有资格基于自己的工作记录获得更高的退休福利。

您是否正在领取基于您父母工作记录的社会保障福利？

如果您工作过，您可能有资格基于自己的工作记录获得更高的残疾福利。

您目前是否未婚，但曾结婚10年或以上？

如果您年满62岁且未婚，并且那段婚姻持续了10年或以上，您可能有资格基于前配偶的工作记录获 得福利。

您的子女是否有资格根据您配偶的工作情况领取社会保障子女福利？

如果您照顾的子女未满16岁或在22岁之前残疾，您可能有资格领取配偶福利。

您目前是否正在领取退休或残疾福利，并且照顾的子女未满18岁或残疾？

您的子女可能根据您的工作情况有资格领取福利。

您是否正在领取补充保障收入（SSI）或社会保障福利，并且有服兵役经历？

如果您曾在美国军队服役，您可能有资格通过退伍军人管理局领取福利。请访问此链接了解更多信 息：http://www.va.gov/

您是否正在领取补充保障收入（SSI），并且您的父母一方已故或正在领取社会保障福利？

如果您未婚且未满18岁或在22岁之前残疾，并且您的父母一方已故或正在领取社会保障福利，您可 能有资格根据您父母的工作情况领取子女福利。

您的收入是否下降或您是否经历了财务资源的损失？

您可能能够通过补充保障收入计划获得额外收入，该计划帮助收入和财务资源有限的老年人和残疾 人。

重要提示：如果您正在领取福利，有某些生活事件您必须报告。如需完整列表，请选择下方适用于 您所领取福利类型的出版物。

注意：未能报告变更可能导致多付款项。

领取退休或遗属福利时您需要了解的事项（第7-13页）

领取社会保障残疾福利时您需要了解的事项（第11-18页）

领取补充保障收入（SSI）时您需要了解的事项（第7-19页）

我们的网站是了解社会保障局所有计划信息的重要资源。您可以在线办理许多事项。

除了使用我们的网站，您还可以拨打我们的免费电话1-800-772-1213。我们对所有通话保密。我们 可以在周一至周五上午7点至下午7点回答具体问题。通常，如果您在周二之后的工作日打电话，等 待时间会更短。我们通过自动电话服务全天24小时提供信息。（您可以使用我们的自动应答系统告 知我们新地址或申请更换医疗保险卡。）如果您失聪或听力困难，您可以拨打我们的TTY号码1-80 0-325-0778。

我们还希望确保您获得准确且礼貌的服务。因此，我们有第二位社会保障代表监听部分电话通话。

# Benefits Planner: Retirement | Benefits For Your Spouse | Social Security Administration

## Benefits Planner: Retirement

### Benefits For Your Spouse

Even if you have never worked under Social Security, you may be able to get spouse s retirement benefits if you are at least 62 years of age and your spouse is receiving retirement or disability benefits. You can also qualify for Medicare at age 65.

If you are divorced, you may still be able to get benefits on your ex-spouse's record. For information on the requirements for Divorced Spouse's Benefits, read "If You Are Divorced

You can receive the spouse's benefit no matter what your age is if you are caring for their child who is also receiving benefits.

### How Much Will I Receive?

If you qualify and apply for your own retirement benefits and for benefits as a spouse, we always pay your own benefits first. If your benefits as a spouse are higher than your own retirement benefits, you will get a combination of benefits equaling the higher spouse benefit.

Your benefits as a spouse do not include any delayed retirement credits your spouse may receive.

If you begin receiving benefits:

- between age 62 and your full retirement age, the amount will be permanently reduced by a percentage based on the number of months up to your full retirement age.

 

- If you are under full retirement age and you continue to work while receiving benefits, your benefits may be affected by the retirement earnings test.

- at your full retirement age, your benefit as a spouse cannot exceed one-half of your spouse's full retirement amount.

 

- If you were born before January 2, 1954 and have already reached full retirement age, you can choose to receive only the spouse s benefit and delay receiving your retirement benefit until a later date. If your spouse is full retirement age and applying for spouse s benefits only, they can apply online by using the retirement application. Your spouse can also contact us to schedule an appointment.

If your spouse s birthday is January 2, 1954 or later, the option to take only one benefit at full retirement age no longer exists. If your spouse files for one benefit, they will be effectively filing for all retirement or spousal benefits.

If you will receive a pension for work not covered by Social Security such as government employment, the amount of your Social Security benefits on your spouse's record may be reduced.

Benefits paid to you as a spouse will not decrease your spouse s retirement benefit. In fact, the value of the benefits you may receive, added to their benefits, may help your spouse decide if taking benefits sooner may be more advantageous.

#### Maximum Family Benefits

If one of your spouse's children also qualifies for benefits, there is a limit to the amount we can pay family members.

The total depends on your spouse's benefit amount and the number of family members who also qualify on the same record. The total varies, but generally the total amount the worker (your spouse) and their family members can receive is about 150 to 180 percent of the worker's full retirement benefit.

If there is an ex-spouse who also qualifies for benefits, they will not affect the total amount of benefits you or your family may receive.

### How Do I Apply?

You can apply:

- Online - Use our Social Security Retirement/Medicare Benefit Application to apply for retirement, spouse's, divorced spouse's or Medicare benefits.

 

- If your spouse is already receiving benefits when you apply, or if you and your spouse apply at the same time, we will also check your eligibility for benefits as a spouse. If you qualify, your application will automatically serve as a request for spousal benefits.

- By phone - Call us at 1-800-772-1213. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call us at TTY 1-800-325-0778.

 

- In person - Visit your local Social Security office. (Call first to make an appointment.)

- If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories you can also - Contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy or consulate.

### Next Steps

Even if you do not qualify for benefits on someone else's record, some members of your family may qualify for benefits on your record. If you:

- are interested in information about benefits for your family, go to "Benefits For Your Family."

- never married or had children, go to "How You Apply For Retirement Benefits Or Medicare."

[Benefits Planner: Survivors | If You Are The Survivor | Social Security Administration > How Your Spouse Earns Social Security Survivors Benefits]
Just as you plan for your family's protection if you die, you should consider the Social Security benefits that may be available if you are the survivor that is, the spouse, child, or parent of a worker who dies. That person must have worked long enough under Social Security to qualify for benefits.

A worker can earn up to four credits each year. In 2019, for example, your spouse can earn one credit for each $1,360 of wages or self-employment income. When your spouse has earned $5,440, they have earned their four credits for the year.

The number of credits needed to provide benefits for survivors depends on the worker's age when they die. No one needs more than 40 credits (10 years of work) to be eligible for any Social Security benefit. But, the younger a person is, the fewer credits they must have for family members to receive survivors benefits.

Benefits can be paid to the worker's children and the surviving spouse who is caring for the children even if the worker doesn't have the required number of credits. They can get benefits if the worker has credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years just before their death. Each person s situation is different and you need to talk to a Social Security claims representative about your choices.

### When A Family Member Dies

We should be notified as soon as possible when a person dies. However, you cannot report a death or apply for survivors benefits online.

In most cases, the funeral home will report the person s death to us. You should give the funeral home the deceased person s Social Security number if you want them to make the report.

If you need to report a death or apply for benefits, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). You can speak to a Social Security representative between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday. You can also visit your local Social Security office. An appointment is not required, but if you call ahead and schedule one, it may reduce the time you spend waiting to speak to someone.

contexts.text:
[Benefits Planner: Survivors | If You Are The Survivor | Social Security Administration > Are other family members eligible? > Other Things You Need To Know]
There are limits on how much survivors may earn while they receive benefits.

Benefits for a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse may be affected by several additional factors:

- If you remarry before you reach age 60 (age 50 if disabled), you cannot receive benefits as a surviving spouse while you are married.
- If you remarry after you reach age 60 (age 50 if disabled), you will continue to qualify for benefits on your deceased spouse's Social Security record.
  However, if your current spouse is a Social Security beneficiary, you may want to apply for spouse's benefits on their record. If that amount is more than your widow's or widower's benefit, you will receive a combination of benefits that equals the higher amount.
- If you receive benefits as a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse, you can switch to your own retirement benefit as early as age 62. This assumes you are eligible for retirement benefits and your retirement rate is higher than your rate as a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse.
- In many cases, a widow or widower can begin receiving one benefit at a reduced rate and then, at full retirement age, switch to the other benefit at an unreduced rate.
- If you will also receive a pension based on work not covered by Social Security, such as government or foreign work, your Social Security benefits as a survivor may be affected.

If your spouse is full retirement age and applying for spouse s benefits only, they can apply online by using the retirement application. Your spouse can also contact us to schedule an appointment.

If your spouse s birthday is January 2, 1954 or later, the option to take only one benefit at full retirement age no longer exists. If your spouse files for one benefit, they will be effectively filing for all retirement or spousal benefits.

If you will receive a pension for work not covered by Social Security such as government employment, the amount of your Social Security benefits on your spouse's record may be reduced.

Benefits paid to you as a spouse will not decrease your spouse s retirement benefit. In fact, the value of the benefits you may receive, added to their benefits, may help your spouse decide if taking benefits sooner may be more advantageous.

#### Maximum Family Benefits

If one of your spouse's children also qualifies for benefits, there is a limit to the amount we can pay family members.

The total depends on your spouse's benefit amount and the number of family members who also qualify on the same record. The total varies, but generally the total amount the worker (your spouse) and their family members can receive is about 150 to 180 percent of the worker's full retirement benefit.

If there is an ex-spouse who also qualifies for benefits, they will not affect the total amount of benefits you or your family may receive.

### How Do I Apply?

You can apply:

- Online - Use our Social Security Retirement/Medicare Benefit Application to apply for retirement, spouse's, divorced spouse's or Medicare benefits.

 

- If your spouse is already receiving benefits when you apply, or if you and your spouse apply at the same time, we will also check your eligibility for benefits as a spouse. If you qualify, your application will automatically serve as a request for spousal benefits.

- By phone - Call us at 1-800-772-1213. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call us at TTY 1-800-325-0778.

 

- In person - Visit your local Social Security office. (Call first to make an appointment.)

- If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories you can also - Contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy or consulate.

### Next Steps

Even if you do not qualify for benefits on someone else's record, some members of your family may qualify for benefits on your record. If you:

- are interested in information about benefits for your family, go to "Benefits For Your Family."

- never married or had children, go to "How You Apply For Retirement Benefits Or Medicare."

# Benefits Planner: Retirement | Benefits For Your Spouse | Social Security Administration

### Benefits For Your Spouse

Even if you have never worked under Social Security, you may be able to get spouse s retirement benefits if you are at least 62 years of age and your spouse is receiving retirement or disability benefits. You can also qualify for Medicare at age 65.

If you are divorced, you may still be able to get benefits on your ex-spouse's record. For information on the requirements for Divorced Spouse's Benefits, read "If You Are Divorced

You can receive the spouse's benefit no matter what your age is if you are caring for their child who is also receiving benefits.

[Benefits Planner: Survivors | If You Are The Survivor | Social Security Administration > How Your Spouse Earns Social Security Survivors Benefits]
Just as you plan for your family's protection if you die, you should consider the Social Security benefits that may be available if you are the survivor that is, the spouse, child, or parent of a worker who dies. That person must have worked long enough under Social Security to qualify for benefits.

A worker can earn up to four credits each year. In 2019, for example, your spouse can earn one credit for each $1,360 of wages or self-employment income. When your spouse has earned $5,440, they have earned their four credits for the year.

The number of credits needed to provide benefits for survivors depends on the worker's age when they die. No one needs more than 40 credits (10 years of work) to be eligible for any Social Security benefit. But, the younger a person is, the fewer credits they must have for family members to receive survivors benefits.

Benefits can be paid to the worker's children and the surviving spouse who is caring for the children even if the worker doesn't have the required number of credits. They can get benefits if the worker has credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years just before their death. Each person s situation is different and you need to talk to a Social Security claims representative about your choices.

### When A Family Member Dies

We should be notified as soon as possible when a person dies. However, you cannot report a death or apply for survivors benefits online.

In most cases, the funeral home will report the person s death to us. You should give the funeral home the deceased person s Social Security number if you want them to make the report.

If you need to report a death or apply for benefits, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). You can speak to a Social Security representative between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday. You can also visit your local Social Security office. An appointment is not required, but if you call ahead and schedule one, it may reduce the time you spend waiting to speak to someone.

[Benefits Planner: Survivors | If You Are The Survivor | Social Security Administration > Are other family members eligible? > Other Things You Need To Know]
There are limits on how much survivors may earn while they receive benefits.

Benefits for a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse may be affected by several additional factors:

- If you remarry before you reach age 60 (age 50 if disabled), you cannot receive benefits as a surviving spouse while you are married.
- If you remarry after you reach age 60 (age 50 if disabled), you will continue to qualify for benefits on your deceased spouse's Social Security record.
  However, if your current spouse is a Social Security beneficiary, you may want to apply for spouse's benefits on their record. If that amount is more than your widow's or widower's benefit, you will receive a combination of benefits that equals the higher amount.
- If you receive benefits as a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse, you can switch to your own retirement benefit as early as age 62. This assumes you are eligible for retirement benefits and your retirement rate is higher than your rate as a widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse.
- In many cases, a widow or widower can begin receiving one benefit at a reduced rate and then, at full retirement age, switch to the other benefit at an unreduced rate.
- If you will also receive a pension based on work not covered by Social Security, such as government or foreign work, your Social Security benefits as a survivor may be affected.

parsed.answer: If your spouse dies, you may be eligible for survivor benefits based on their work record. Generally, you can receive survivor benefits as a widow/widower if you are at least age 60 (age 50 if disabled), or at any age if you are caring for their child who is under 16 or disabled.
